\section{Strengths, Weaknesses and Trade-offs}
\label{sec:pros-cons}

The previous section explained why Michelangelo was designed the way it
was. This section evaluates the outcome. We draw mainly on
Uber's own engineering blog posts, which are unusually candid about what
did not work. We first list the main strengths and weaknesses, then
summarise the lessons Uber itself reported, state the key trade-offs
explicitly, and finally compare Michelangelo with two well-known
alternatives: Google TFX and Netflix Metaflow.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Strengths}
\label{subsec:strengths}

\paragraph{S1. Feature reuse across teams.}
Uber observed that many modelling problems use identical or similar
features, so it built a shared feature store in which teams publish
features with only a small amount of extra metadata (owner, description,
SLA) and consume them by referencing a canonical name in the model
configuration~\cite{delbalso2017meet}. The platform then joins the
right offline data for training and fetches the right online values at
prediction time. The store held about 10{,}000 features in
2017~\cite{delbalso2017meet}; by 2024 its successor, Palette, hosted
more than 20{,}000 features available out of the box~\cite{wang2024predictive}.
Reuse removes duplicated pipeline work, which matters because building
data pipelines is one of the most costly parts of an ML
solution~\cite{delbalso2017meet}.

\paragraph{S2. A standardised, end-to-end workflow.}
Michelangelo replaced team-specific scripts and custom serving containers
with one six-step workflow (manage data, train, evaluate, deploy, predict,
monitor) that applies to classification, regression and time-series
problems alike~\cite{delbalso2017meet}. Standardisation shows up in
concrete mechanisms: every trained model is stored as a versioned record
with its configuration, data references and metrics~\cite{delbalso2017meet};
deployment and monitoring sit behind a single click in the
UI~\cite{delbalso2018scaling}; and a new model can be deployed to the same
\emph{tag} as an old one, so that client services switch models without
any code change~\cite{delbalso2017meet}. Michelangelo~2.0 extended
this discipline to code: model code and configuration live in a version-controlled
monorepo with code review and CI/CD, including changes made
through the UI~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

\paragraph{S3. Scalability.}
Because models are stateless, online serving scales horizontally by
adding hosts behind a load balancer, and batch scoring scales by adding
Spark executors~\cite{delbalso2017meet}. In 2017 Uber reported P95
latency below 5\,ms for models that need no stored features and below
10\,ms for models that read from the Cassandra feature store, with the
busiest models serving over 250{,}000 predictions per
second~\cite{delbalso2017meet}. By 2024 the platform managed about
400 active projects, more than 20{,}000 training jobs per month and more
than 5{,}000 production models, serving up to 10 million real-time
predictions per second at peak~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

\paragraph{S4. Project tiering.}
Michelangelo~2.0 introduced a four-level tiering scheme: tier~1 covers
models in core trip and eater flows such as ETA, safety and fraud
detection, while tier~4 covers experimental use
cases~\cite{wang2024predictive}. The tier determines resource
investment, outage handling and how strictly best practices are enforced.
This fixed a weakness of version~1.0, where every project was treated the
same and high-impact projects were under-invested~\cite{wang2024predictive}.
Tiering is paired with the Model Excellence Score, which applies the SLA
concept from site reliability engineering to model quality (accuracy,
freshness, feature quality)~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Weaknesses}
\label{subsec:weaknesses}

\paragraph{W1. Heavyweight for prototyping.}
The first version was built around Apache Spark for large-scale processing
and training and Java for low-latency serving, because the most urgent use
cases were very high scale~\cite{delbalso2018scaling}. Uber admits this
structure worked well for production but carried overhead and lacked
flexibility and ease of use during early prototyping~\cite{delbalso2018scaling}.
Every supported model type is built into the training and serving systems,
so these systems depend on the libraries of all model types, and the
dependency graph grows with each type added~\cite{uber2018pyml}. Adding a
new algorithm means extending the training, deployment and serving
components, and a custom transformation means preprocessing the data in
Hive or extending the DSL, which Uber calls ``a fairly invasive
operation''~\cite{uber2018pyml}.
Version~1.0 also had weak deep-learning support: teams such as Maps ETA
had to spend months building their own DL toolkits before training a first
DL model~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

\paragraph{W2. Centralisation creates a large blast radius and a bottleneck.}
A central platform means that one fault can affect many teams at once. In
2021 a bad change to Palette's shared metadata, which was not caught
because schema validation ran only on the client side, prevented the
online serving stack from loading metadata at start-up and broke major
tier-1 use cases~\cite{uber2024palette}. Recovery took several hours,
partly because a change to one feature group triggered updates to all
feature groups~\cite{uber2024palette}. Centralisation also creates an
organisational bottleneck: when requirements outpaced the platform
roadmap, product teams were tempted to build their own systems, and Uber
needed a group of senior leaders to prevent fragmentation and technical
debt~\cite{delbalso2018scaling}. Fragmentation happened anyway; under version~1.0 teams
used several semi-isolated tools (DSW, ML Explorer, uFlow/uScorer), each
with different UI patterns~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

\paragraph{W3. Tight coupling to Uber's in-house infrastructure.}
Michelangelo is an internal service built on top of Uber's own data lake,
Kafka brokers, Samza streaming engine, managed Cassandra clusters and
in-house service provisioning and deployment tools~\cite{delbalso2017meet}.
Even in 2024 its compute clusters were still being migrated from
Peloton/Mesos to Kubernetes~\cite{wang2024predictive}.
This coupling is what makes the platform fast inside Uber, but it means
the design cannot be adopted as a product by other organisations, and
each infrastructure migration becomes a platform-wide project.

\paragraph{W4. Scala, configuration and UI workflows slowed experimentation.}
Early feature transformations were written in a DSL implemented as a
subset of Scala~\cite{delbalso2017meet}, and models were configured
through a web UI or configuration files. Uber reports that this focus led
it away from the mature programmatic interfaces that model developers
already knew, even though modelling is highly
iterative~\cite{delbalso2018scaling}. Uber calls this ``an explicitly chosen
trade-off to favor performance and scalability over flexibility'' that made
it hard for data science teams to iterate quickly on new
models~\cite{uber2018pyml}. In version~1.0, collaboration in the UI
and notebooks relied on manual copying and merging, without version
control, branching or code review~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Lessons Reported by Uber}
\label{subsec:lessons}

Uber's own retrospectives name several lessons. We highlight four that
directly explain the strengths and weaknesses above.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Data is the hardest part of ML.} Modellers spend most of
  their time selecting and transforming features and building pipelines to
  deliver them to production, and broken data is the most common cause of
  problems in production ML systems~\cite{delbalso2018scaling}. This is the
  main justification for investing in the feature store (S1).

  \item \textbf{Making open-source components work at scale is expensive.}
  Although Spark and Cassandra are mature projects, it took more than a
  year of sustained effort for \emph{each} of them to work reliably at
  Uber's scale; some commercial toolkits tried early on were
  abandoned~\cite{delbalso2018scaling}.

  \item \textbf{Shared metadata needs server-side safeguards.} After the
  2021 Palette incident, Uber spent more than a year re-architecting the
  metadata store: it defined a formal object model, moved validation to
  the server, processed only incremental changes, and added a wrapper
  with a kill switch for fast rollback~\cite{uber2024palette}. As a result,
  onboarding deployment time dropped by more than 95\% and end-to-end
  metadata updates went from over an hour to about 15
  minutes~\cite{uber2024palette}.

  \item \textbf{Offer a hybrid: an easy option and a high-scale option.}
  Uber concluded it should let developers use the tools they want, and
  settled on offering a high-scale option that is harder to use alongside
  a lower-scale option that is very easy to use~\cite{delbalso2018scaling}.
PyML was the first example: any Python model can be packaged and deployed
quickly, and once it proves its value and needs high-scale online serving,
it can be re-implemented natively in Michelangelo for lower latency and
better resource efficiency~\cite{uber2018pyml}.
  The 2024 architecture generalises this: MA Studio serves standard
  workflows without code, while Canvas gives power users code-level access
  for advanced cases such as deep learning~\cite{wang2024predictive}.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Key Trade-offs}
\label{subsec:tradeoffs}

The strengths and weaknesses are two sides of the same design decisions.
We state the three most important ones explicitly.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Scale and standardisation vs.\ iteration speed.}
  Building on Spark, Java and a Scala DSL \emph{gained} reliable,
  high-throughput production pipelines and consistent features between
  training and serving~\cite{delbalso2017meet}, but \emph{lost}
  developer velocity during prototyping~\cite{delbalso2018scaling,uber2018pyml}.

  \item \textbf{Centralisation vs.\ resilience and autonomy.}
  A single platform and a single feature store \emph{gained} reuse,
  governance and consistent quality standards~\cite{wang2024predictive},
  but \emph{lost} fault isolation (one metadata change affected many
  tier-1 services~\cite{uber2024palette}) and made product teams dependent
  on the platform roadmap~\cite{delbalso2018scaling}.

  \item \textbf{End-to-end convenience vs.\ flexibility.}
  An integrated workflow \emph{gained} a fast path for common use cases,
  but \emph{lost} flexibility for specialised domains, which pushed Uber
  to start factoring out an explicit infrastructure layer for teams building their
  own platforms~\cite{delbalso2018scaling} and to allow ``bring your own''
  components outside the managed subset~\cite{wang2024predictive}.
\end{itemize}

A related trade-off concerns model choice: deep learning \emph{gains}
accuracy on complex problems but \emph{costs} significant infrastructure,
and Uber notes that in several cases XGBoost outperformed DL in both
performance and cost~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

\subsection{Comparison with TFX and Metaflow}
\label{subsec:comparison}

\Cref{tab:platform-comparison} compares Michelangelo with Google's
TensorFlow Extended (TFX)~\cite{baylor2017tfx,tfxguide} and Netflix's
Metaflow~\cite{metaflowdocs}. The key distinction is between a
\emph{centralised platform} operated by a dedicated team and a
\emph{library or framework} that each adopting team runs on its own
infrastructure.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \small
  \caption{Michelangelo compared with TFX and Metaflow.}
  \label{tab:platform-comparison}
  \begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.6cm}
                               >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X
                               >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X
                               >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X}
    \toprule
    \textbf{Criterion} & \textbf{Michelangelo (Uber)} &
    \textbf{TFX (Google)} & \textbf{Metaflow (Netflix)} \\
    \midrule
    Type &
      Centralised internal ML-as-a-service platform~\cite{delbalso2017meet} &
      Pipeline framework of standard components and
      libraries~\cite{tfxguide} &
      Python library with a unified API over the
      infrastructure stack~\cite{metaflowdocs} \\
    \addlinespace
    Availability &
      Internal to Uber only~\cite{delbalso2017meet} &
      Open source; originated as Google's internal
      platform~\cite{baylor2017tfx,tfxguide} &
      Open source (Apache~2.0)~\cite{metaflowdocs} \\
    \addlinespace
    Who operates it &
      Dedicated Michelangelo platform team~\cite{delbalso2018scaling} &
      The adopting team, on its chosen orchestrator~\cite{tfxguide} &
      The adopting team, on its own cloud or Kubernetes
      account~\cite{metaflowdocs} \\
    \addlinespace
    ML frameworks &
      Multi-framework: Spark ML, XGBoost, TensorFlow, PyTorch,
      LLMs~\cite{wang2024predictive} &
      Centred on TensorFlow~\cite{baylor2017tfx} &
      Any Python library~\cite{metaflowdocs} \\
    \addlinespace
    Feature management &
      Shared feature store (Palette) with offline and online
      stores~\cite{wang2024predictive} &
      Transform component applies the same preprocessing in training and
      serving; feature sharing is not a core component~\cite{tfxguide} &
      Patterns for reading from warehouses and lakes; a feature store is
      not among the layers it covers~\cite{metaflowdocs} \\
    \addlinespace
    Online serving &
      Built-in low-latency prediction service (P95 under
      10\,ms)~\cite{delbalso2017meet} &
      Serving infrastructure is part of the
      platform~\cite{baylor2017tfx} &
      ``Deployment'' means production workflow orchestration; online
      serving is left to other tools~\cite{metaflowdocs} \\
    \addlinespace
    Orchestration and compute &
      Kubernetes-style control plane; Spark and Ray
      jobs~\cite{wang2024predictive} &
      Apache Airflow, Apache Beam, Kubeflow
      Pipelines~\cite{tfxguide} &
      AWS Batch, Step Functions, Kubernetes, Argo,
      Airflow~\cite{metaflowdocs} \\
    \addlinespace
    Developer experience &
      Web UI (MA Studio) plus code-driven workflows
      (Canvas)~\cite{wang2024predictive} &
      Python pipeline definitions~\cite{tfxguide} &
      Local-first Python; prototype on a laptop, then
      scale~\cite{metaflowdocs} \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Discussion.}
The comparison shows two different answers to the same problem. Both
Michelangelo and TFX were created because ad-hoc glue code and
team-specific scripts made ML fragile and slow to reach
production~\cite{delbalso2017meet,baylor2017tfx}, and Metaflow was
built to raise data-scientist productivity from prototype to
production~\cite{metaflowdocs}.
Michelangelo answers with a centralised service that owns the whole
lifecycle, including a feature store and a low-latency serving tier.
This gives Uber the deepest integration and the strongest guarantees
against training--serving skew, but at the cost of portability and a
heavy dependence on one platform team. TFX and Metaflow answer with
reusable building blocks that each team assembles and operates on
infrastructure it already has, which makes them portable but leaves
feature management and, in Metaflow's case, online serving to other
tools. Interestingly, the designs are converging: Michelangelo~2.0
moved towards plug-and-play components and code-first workflows that
resemble a framework~\cite{wang2024predictive}, while TFX itself began as
a centralised internal platform at Google~\cite{baylor2017tfx}. For an
organisation of Uber's size, with hundreds of projects and strict latency
requirements, a central platform pays off; for smaller teams, a library
such as Metaflow offers most of the workflow benefits without the cost of
building and running a platform.
